title: A court that almost never executed (Mishnah Makkot 1:10)
hookLine: a court that executed once in seven years was called destructive; some said once in seventy

cards: A court that puts someone to death once in seven years is called destructive.

That's a sentence from the Mishnah, in the tractate Makkot, and it comes from inside the system, from the rabbis who taught the laws of the court. Then another voice: Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah says, once in seventy years.
Then Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: if we had sat on the court, no one would ever have been put to death.

teach.b: Sanhedrin. The Mishnah's name for the great court, and the name of the tractate that lays out how it works. The Torah does name crimes that carry death.
The Mishnah keeps those laws, then builds a court that leans hard the other way. Three of its rules. First, the order of speaking.
Capital cases open with reasons to acquit, not to convict, and anyone may argue for the accused. Second, the clock. Acquittal may be given the same day.
A verdict of guilt waits until the next day, so the judges sleep on it. Third, the road. The Mishnah describes someone at the door of the court with a cloth in hand, and a rider posted at a distance.

teach.h: A CLOTH WAVES, A RIDER STOPS IT.
teach.b: If anyone comes forward with something in the accused's favor, the cloth waves, the rider gallops off, and the procession stops. Even on the way out, the case can reopen.

teach.h: SEVEN, SEVENTY, NEVER, AND A WARNING.
teach.b: Then the argument in Makkot: seven years, seventy, never. And the Mishnah doesn't let that last word stand alone.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel answers Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva: then you would multiply murderers in Israel. A court that never acts doesn't protect anyone either. Both voices stay on the page.
Some readers take all this as a memory of how courts once ran; others, as a picture of what a court ought to be.
Either way, when a life hangs in the balance, the system tilts toward keeping it.

how: Jews study the tractates Sanhedrin and Makkot as part of the Talmud's order of damages, and the debate in Makkot 1:10 is often cited in Jewish discussions of justice and the death penalty.

games.q: you're on the court. the accused is being led out, and someone runs up saying they have something to say in his favor. what happens?
o: the cloth waves, the rider stops the procession, and the case reopens.
the judges note it for the record.
games.why: the Mishnah posts a person with a cloth at the court's door and a rider in the distance, so a new argument can stop everything, even on the road.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've been judging lately, a coworker, a relative, a stranger online, and play the person at the court's door.
Find one thing to say in their favor, something you don't know about their day or something they did right, and let it be heard first. Then notice whether the verdict feels quite as finished.

wordCard.voice: Sanhedrin. The great court of the Mishnah, where the case for acquittal speaks first and a verdict of guilt waits a night. Today's word.
